claim: Directional microstructures reduce drag primarily through elastic deformation that reduces the effective contact area with the fluid.
mechanism: The microstructures are designed to flex under flow pressure, creating a dynamic surface that reduces the effective contact area with the fluid. This flexibility allows the surface to temporarily align with flow streamlines, reducing drag through a combination of reduced contact area and improved flow alignment.
evidence: Fish skin scales have some flexibility that affects flow
Elastic surfaces can reduce drag in certain conditions
Dynamic surfaces can adapt to flow conditions
assumptions: The polymer microstructures can deform elastically under operational pressures
Deformation reduces effective contact area without increasing turbulence
Recovery after deformation is rapid and complete
expected_failure_modes: Reduced effectiveness over time due to material fatigue
Increased drag from feature misalignment after deformation
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis introduces surface flexibility and dynamic adaptation as the primary mechanism, rather than static structural features.
testability: Can be tested using high-speed imaging to measure surface deformation under flow and correlating deformation with drag reduction.
falsifier: If microstructured pipes show no measurable deformation under operational pressures but still maintain reduced drag, this hypothesis is wrong.
